title: Paint touches
lead: How getting the ball into the key relates to shot quality, turnovers, free throws and offensive rebounds, in the ten tracked games.

blocks.text: When the offense gets the ball into the key, what happens to the rest of the chance? This tab compares chances with and without a **paint touch**: a touch whose SkillCorner regions include the key or the restricted area, before the chance's shot. The unit is the **chance** (an offensive rebound starts a new one), because shot quality, turnovers, free throws and offensive rebounds are decided per chance.

Check of the flag against the tracking: on 98% of SkillCorner's paint touches the ball holder is tracked inside the key at some frame of the touch; of the touches where he is tracked inside it, SkillCorner flags 83%. The flag is used as delivered; the tracked entry frame times it.

Chances that reach the paint differ in many ways from those that do not (they last longer, they come against different defenses, the shooters are different). Every comparison here is an association in ten games, not the effect of forcing a paint touch.

blocks.text: All chances, split by whether the ball got into the key. blocks.title: turnover rate
blocks.unit: of chances end in a turnover

blocks.text: With a paint touch the offense scored 1.02 points per chance against 0.65 without; turnovers 10% vs 15%, free-throw trips 14% vs 9%. Shot quality per FGA: 1.05 vs 0.97 xPts. Live misses were rebounded by the offense 32% vs 30% of the time.

blocks.text: On drives the defense pulls in as the ball enters: 0.8 defenders in the key 2 s before the entry, 2.8 one second after; the defense's hull shrinks from 306 to 147 sq ft. The attackers away from the ball gain room (nearest defender 7.8 ft before, 8.9 ft at the entry), which is the raw material for the kick-out threes above.

sections.title: What this shows and does not

blocks.text: It shows how often the ball gets into the key, how it gets there, what the defense does in the next two seconds and how the chance ends. It does not show that a paint touch causes better outcomes: good offenses, bad defenses and long chances all produce more paint touches.

Next steps if this becomes the topic: compare paint touches within the same team and lineup; separate a touch that ends the chance (layup, foul) from one that moves the defense (kick-out), since the first is mostly shot location; and test whether the defense's contraction predicts the next shot's openness beyond where it is taken.
